newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels free more hostages, insist on demands.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels free more hostages, insist on demands.

text.p: Marxist rebels on Friday night released 38 of the roughly 400 hostages they were holding inside the besieged Japanese ambassador's home in Peru but vowed not to surrender until their demands were met.
As the hostage crisis entered its fourth day, the freed men emerged from the mansion under the glare of television lights and photographers' flashes. At least two had to be pushed out in wheelchairs.

Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas masterminding the siege sent a message with the group promising that a "significant" number of extra hostages would be freed if the government allowed the rebels to speak by telephone with their comrades imprisoned in Peruvian jails.
But the hostage-takers stood firm on their main demand for the release of all jailed MRTA members -- something President Alberto Fujimori's government has already rejected.
"We repeat that the only possible solution is that of listening to our positions and proceeding to free all those (guerrillas) detained," the rebel statement said.
Opposition congressman Javier Diez Canseco said the main message from inside the residence was:"The situation is bad."
Adding to the gloom, Canadian ambassador Anthony Vincent -- himself a freed captive -- told Canadian Broadcasting Corp television that "There's still a very long way to go before the crisis ends."
Peru had earlier ignored desperate pleas by captives for vital services to be restored to the besieged residence -- a message repeated Friday night by the freed hostages.
Neither handwritten signs thrust at a residence window requesting water, electricity and telephone service nor reports of worsening hostage health appeared to move Fujimori.
As Peruvians prayed for the lives of the captives, their president spent much of the day huddled with generals at a military barracks.

Three days after the daring assault, the roughly 20 MRTA rebels still held around 360 hostages in worsening health, including at least eight ambassadors, two Peruvian cabinet ministers and around 40 Japanese businessmen.
Envoys from Brazil, South Korea and Egypt were among the 38 freed Friday night.
Red Cross officials said early on Friday some of the captives were suffering from diarrhoea, diabetes, ulcers and heart problems inside the cramped, sweaty residence.
Citizens across this poor Andean nation clustered around radio sets and televisions in bars, shops and cafes hungrily seeking the latest word on the hostages' fate.

Japan and the United States both pushed Peru to seek a peaceful solution to the crisis and put hostages' lives first. Tokyo sent Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda to Lima to push a cautious, go-slow approach in negotiations with the MRTA.
Fujimori assured President Bill Clinton he would do so but the true intentions of the enigmatic Peruvian leader, better known for strong-arm tactics than diplomacy, were unclear.

His prime minister Alberto Pandolfi kept hopes up by telling reporters that the government hoped for a peaceful end to the crisis, but police sources said preparations for a commando-style raid were being considered as one option.
Under international law the besieged residence is considered Japanese territory so Fujimori must seek Tokyo's permission before taking any military action.
Negotiations by the Red Cross and a team of diplomats over the past two days resulted in the entry of food, water and much-needed portable toilets on Friday into the residence.

Inside, the hostages -- who include Peru's anti-terrorism chief and its Foreign Minister -- faced their fourth straight night sleeping on the floor in crumpled suits and sharing meagre rations under the watchful gaze of their captors.

Adding to the tension, a man claiming to be an MRTA rebel phoned Lima's CPN radio station to warn authorities against a raid on the residence. "We don't want any attack or any assault," the unidentified caller said. "We know we're dead anyway and there's nothing left but for us all to die together."
Anxious relatives, some of whom prayed through the night for their loved ones waited outside in the hope of news. A big candlelit vigil was planned for the evening in a park near the residence.
Japan's Ikeda engaged in 20 hours of hectic non-stop diplomacy with the large Japanese community, the Canadian mediator and the U.S. ambassador but aides had no comment on the results.

So far, Fujimori's hard line against the rebels seemed popular with ordinary Peruvians, who are fed up with guerrilla violence. Citizens up and down the country hoisted national flags on makeshift masts or draped them from windows to show their support for the government.
